People / tribal nation

Kiowa

Kiowa histories connect northern and southern Plains movement, Texas and Oklahoma, while the present Kiowa Tribe publishes accounts of its government and community institutions. This foundation brings a short Tribal history together with an edited treaty, dated education reporting, a Kiowa educator’s first-person reflection, a collaborative scholarly account and art history. Alliances, the wider people, present institutions and individual voices retain their own scope.

Still unfinished

Six substantive actual-content works provide a useful first foundation across institutional history, a primary treaty, contemporary education, first-person language work, collaborative pedagogy and art history. Three supporting/navigation records are excluded. The history remains uneven, primary Texas implementation records are unread, early chronology conflicts and current-governance detail remain open. Quantity does not establish adequate coverage, completion or community endorsement.

Assessment recorded October 26, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • Early origins, migration dates and archaeological identifications need stronger comparison. The Tribal history’s Black Hills date and Kracht’s date differ; no precise origin conclusion is settled here.
  • Nineteenth-century Texas diplomacy, warfare, captivity, removal and reservation implementation need directly inspected Kiowa perspectives and primary records beyond the single edited treaty.
  • Allotment, land loss and later government history need specifically dated legal/historical sources. No current landownership, jurisdiction, citizenship or benefits determination is made.
  • The annual report is a selected-page first-party institutional account, not a complete report review or independent outcomes audit; figures and program guarantees were deliberately omitted.
  • First-person educational aims and published recollections are situated perspectives. The teacher-training notice is dated, and apps, recordings, live classes and language-proficiency outcomes were not tested.
  • Art-group membership is introduced, but artist biographies, dates, community meanings and image rights require more work. No artwork reproduction right follows from a linked essay.
  • Private family documents, raw interviews and restricted underlying materials were not accessed. Published culturally governed stories, songs and sensitive-place details were excluded from the synthesis and were not reproduced.
  • The six-work collection remains uneven across historical periods and community perspectives. No community review, endorsement, comprehensive coverage or research completion is claimed.

Téh-tóot-sah (better known as Tohausen, Little Bluff), First Chief, 1834
George Catlin, 1834. Smithsonian American Art Museum, Gift of Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Jr., 1985.66.62. Public domain.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — SAAM item marked Free to use

Smithsonian American Art Museum identifies the sitter as Téh-tóot-sah, also known as Tohausen or Little Bluff, a Kiowa chief, and dates George Catlin’s oil portrait to 1834. Its actual subject classification explicitly names Kiowa. This is an outside artist’s historical portrait of an individually identified person, not a generic Native likeness, a documentary photograph, Kiowa-made art, or a current tribal-government representative. Exact portrait location, clothing/design meanings, current cultural practice and community endorsement are not established by this image check. The named leader and date are retained without claiming that one person represents all Kiowa communities or periods. Complete 2466x3000 museum-delivered source JPEG inspected and preserved. Web copy resized proportionally to 1480x1800 and recompressed at quality 88; no pixel crop, added detail, generated material, retouching or recoloring. Cards and opened-page backgrounds may use disclosed CSS crops/overlays. Preserve a full-frame route where possible. CSS crops and overlays apply to directory/background copies; the opened-page image retains the complete delivered frame.

01

A people, a present Tribe and related reading routes

Kiowa is a people-level reading route, while the Kiowa Tribe’s publications describe a present government and its institutions in Oklahoma. The Tribe’s history discusses alliances with Comanche and Plains Apache people. Those relationships do not make the names interchangeable: Plains Apache has its own directory route, and shared treaties or institutions do not by themselves establish one timeless identity.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [3] Kiowa Tribe

02

Movement, Texas connections and uncertain early dates

The Tribe’s historical account and Kracht’s article both describe movement from the northern toward the southern Plains and connections with present-day Texas. Their Black Hills chronologies differ. These accounts provide a broad route into the history; precise origins, dates and archaeological identifications need further research. The Atlas does not turn a migration outline into a fixed homeland boundary or treat a community history page as an inspected archaeological report.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [8] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture

03

Horses, bison and historical livelihoods

The Tribe’s overview describes historical mobility, bison hunting, horse use and gathering. Read that account in its period and regional setting. It helps explain the Southern Plains history being discussed, while contemporary education, work and family life require their own sources rather than a picture of every Kiowa person living in one historical way.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe

04

Reading the 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty

The edited October 21, 1867 Kiowa and Comanche treaty includes reservation and conditional hunting provisions, promises of federal services, a requirement concerning later land cessions and compulsory schooling in English branches. Its terms give readers a primary document to examine. They do not alone prove implementation, universal consent or present-day rights. This named instrument should also be distinguished from the separate treaty involving Kiowa, Comanche and Apache representatives.

Read the sources [5] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

05

Reservation change and the limits of this first history

The Tribal history and Kracht’s account describe reservation confinement, allotment and settlement pressures. Their compressed narratives are starting points for reviewing nineteenth-century Texas and Oklahoma history. The original military, removal, allotment and implementation records have not been read in this foundation, so precise legal conclusions, landownership totals and a complete chronology remain open.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [8] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [5] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

06

Education as a contemporary institution

The Tribe’s FY 2025–2026 report describes its Education Agency across child care, school partnerships, higher education, career learning and community activities. It presents Kiowa language, heritage and contemporary life as part of its educational aims. These are the institution’s reported purposes and activities. The Atlas does not promise assistance, repeat financial figures or treat the report as an independent evaluation of results.

Read the sources [3] Kiowa Tribe

07

Language teaching across classrooms and families

The same dated report describes a teacher-credentialing process and language classes delivered in schools, community settings and online. Melody Windsong Redbird-Post’s first-person essay gives another perspective: she recounts child-care language work, family learning and collaboration with elders, educators and parents. Her experience and future project plans remain attributed to her; neither source supplies a verified current count of speakers or proof of every learner’s proficiency.

Read the sources [3] Kiowa Tribe [4] LearnKiowa [9] Kiowa Tribe, Kiowa Language Department

08

Community listening and a shared classroom

In their 2018 article, Rachel C. Jackson with Kiowa Elder Dorothy Whitehorse DeLaune describe the Kiowa Clemente course and a classroom shaped by community interests. Their account explains how listening, shared decisions and language work inform their teaching. This is a situated educational interpretation and relationship, not a rule for every Kiowa person or a present course schedule. Specific stories, songs and culturally governed materials in the publication are not retold here.

Read the sources [6] Community Literacy Journal; public copy hosted by University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma

09

Named artists and the Kiowa Six

Lydia L. Wyckoff’s art-historical essay identifies Jack Hokeah, Monroe Tsatoke, Spencer Asah, James Auchiah, Stephen Mopope and Lois Smoky within the group known as the Kiowa Six or Kiowa Five. It follows their painting, university-era work and mural commissions. The essay describes plain backgrounds and areas of flat color as part of this history. These are named artists and an art-group label; the account does not define all Kiowa art or authorize reuse of the artworks.

Read the sources [7] Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, University of Nebraska–Lincoln; author affiliation printed as Philbrook Museum of Art

10

Reading path and unfinished coverage

Begin with the Tribe’s history, keeping its limits visible, and compare the actual 1867 treaty text. The annual report, Redbird-Post’s essay and the community-listening article offer different routes into education and continuing language work. Follow the art-history essay to named creative lives. Six substantive works form a first foundation; primary Texas records, broader Kiowa-authored history and careful source comparison remain needed. No community review or completed history is claimed.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [5] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties [3] Kiowa Tribe [4] LearnKiowa [6] Community Literacy Journal; public copy hosted by University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma [7] Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, University of Nebraska–Lincoln; author affiliation printed as Philbrook Museum of Art

The Tribe’s own account follows movement, alliances, horse/bison-based life and reservation change. It is a useful short community-published orientation. Exact early dates, archaeology and present landownership claims require comparison; the page is not independent verification of its referenced history.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, October 21, 1867 — edited primary text ↗

Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, October 21, 1867. 15 Stat. 581. Ratified July 25, 1868; proclaimed August 25, 1868. Oklahoma State University Libraries edited transcription.

Publication: 1867-10-21

The actual text places reservation and conditional hunting provisions beside federal services and compulsory schooling. It gives readers a primary agreement to examine while keeping historical terminology, consent and implementation questions open. The same treaty in another profile or edition remains one underlying work.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual HTML dating/preamble, Articles 1–16 and signatory headings; close reading of Articles 2, 7, 11, 12 and 16. Reviewed directly during this session’s independent Comanche QA and applied here with explicit Kiowa scope. Manuscript images, translations, negotiations, ratification documents and later legal interpretation not independently inspected.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access status: Public searchable English HTML

Access note: The text includes an editorial note about pencil/ink brackets. The draft does not infer universal consent, fulfillment, present treaty rights, current jurisdiction, citizenship or legal advice. The October 21 Kiowa/Comanche treaty is not silently treated as the separate Kiowa/Comanche/Apache instrument.

https://treaties.okstate.edu/treaties/treaty-with-the-kiowa-and-comanche-1867-0977

Decolonizing Community Writing with Community Listening: Story, Transrhetorical Resistance, and Indigenous Cultural Literacy Activism — selected teaching/method sections ↗

Jackson, Rachel C., with Dorothy Whitehorse DeLaune. 2018. “Decolonizing Community Writing with Community Listening: Story, Transrhetorical Resistance, and Indigenous Cultural Literacy Activism.” Community Literacy Journal, fall, 37–54. Selected sections.

Publication: 2018

The authors describe a community-shaped Kiowa Clemente course and explain their approach to collaborative listening. Their interpretation and situated recollections are attributed, rather than adopted as a general rule for all Kiowa people. Sacred or seasonally governed stories in the paper are not retold.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual PDF title/abstract; teaching collaboration and author-position account on printed pp. 37–38; course-development/pedagogy discussion pp. 48–50, stopping before the specific seasonal-story discussion; closing methodological discussion encountered on pp. 52–53; author identification on p. 54. Other passages returned with those windows were encountered, but detailed narrated stories, quoted songs, private family documents and raw interviews were not independently researched or reproduced. The full 18-page paper is not claimed as systematically reviewed.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access status: Public searchable English PDF; no account required

Access note: PDF running header says fall 2018; printed pages 37–54 verified. The article is an interpretive educational study, not an independent verification of each historical anecdote or a current attendance survey. Its explicit cultural access/timing concerns are respected by not reproducing stories, songs, ritual details or sensitive places.

Kiowa Six — art-historical essay ↗

A substantial museum-authored encyclopedia essay identifies six artists, including Lois Smoky, and follows painting, patronage and public mural work. It helps introduce named creative lives. Its broad gender generalizations and inconsistent biographical/allotment dates are not adopted without further comparison.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual complete main essay, author line and reference, lines 12–31. Used only for named group membership and attributed account of flat-color painting, university-era work and mural patronage. Images and the cited 1996 book were not inspected.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access status: Public English HTML

Access note: Some artist birth dates differ from Smithsonian catalogue results encountered in discovery, and the essay’s allotment chronology differs from other history sources; the draft omits those precise dates. “Kiowa Five” and “Kiowa Six” are art-group labels, not names of new tribes. Generalized claims about women’s artistic roles are not projected onto all people or periods.

https://plainshumanities.unl.edu/encyclopedia/doc/egp.art.042.html
